title: A bounded, defaults-holding loss that the published recipe still cannot reproduce
rationale:
The per-row recipe verdict is a tri-state column across the whole corpus, and a column that always answers YES is a column that does nothing. This is the purpose-built NO case, so the control is proven live from a fixture the corpus owns rather than from whichever existing row happens to diverge this month. Under maxDepth(2) the subtree below a_b is truncated to JSON text; the row reconstructs identically through the DEFAULT reconstructor, so the existing defaults arm answers YES - and a consumer following the published recipe verbatim gets a completely different document, because the page's flattener runs at its own default depth. That gap is the whole reason the recipe column exists: the defaults arm re-reconstructs a map the fixture's flattener already produced and is structurally blind to any divergence the FLATTENER creates.

TWO PREDICTIONS WERE WRONG HERE AND BOTH ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY FIXED. First, depth-overflow-aliases-a-real-string was expected to flip to recipe=NO and does not: its leaf is a string at depth 3, inside its own maxDepth(3), so a default flatten produces the identical map. Second, this row was predicted LOSSLESS on the theory that a truncated subtree round-trips as its own text. It does not: the BASELINE is the original nested object, not the truncated one, so truncation is lossy by construction - the same mechanism depth-one-over-max already publishes as ACCEPTED_LOSS. Measurement wins; the classification was corrected and an override records the disagreement.
catchesBugClass: The specific misleading shape this gap is about: a row published as holding under defaults which a consumer following the published recipe verbatim cannot reproduce. It proves the recipe verdict can return NO for a FLATTENER-side divergence, which is the class the defaults arm cannot see at all.
cannotCatch: It proves the column can say NO for a flattener-side divergence only. It cannot prove the column discriminates correctly across every other row, and it cannot prove the verdict is right where it says NOT_APPLICABLE - that population is pinned by a count gate, not by this fixture. Its LOSS is not an independent finding: the truncation mechanism duplicates depth-one-over-max exactly, and this row earns its place as the recipe control rather than as evidence of a second depth bug.

predicted.detail: Predicted LOSSLESS on the theory that the truncated subtree round-trips as its own text. MEASURED LOSSY: the baseline is the original nested object, so a_b comes back as a string where the source had an object. The prediction is kept verbatim, the manifest publishes the measurement, and classificationOverrides records the disagreement.
